title: The Taizé chants
hookLine: short, repeated chants from an ecumenical community of brothers in a French village
last: THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.

lines: A LOW CHURCH, CANDLES ON THE FLOOR.
cards: Ubi caritas et amor. A long, low church, almost dark, with candles on the floor up front and people sitting on the ground, a lot of them young, backpacks against the wall. A line is sung.
It ends. It starts again. Same words, same tune.
And again. Nobody's in a hurry for verse two, because there isn't one. After a while, people stop reading the words off the sheet.
A while longer, and some have their eyes closed. This is evening prayer in Taizé, a small village in France. Yesterday the sound of prayer was silence.

teach.b: Taizé is home to a community of brothers, men who live together under vows, founded by a Swiss Protestant known as Brother Roger.
From the start it was meant to be ecumenical, a place where Christians from different churches could pray together.
Today the brothers come from Protestant and Catholic backgrounds, and young people come to spend a week living and praying with them.

First, the chants are short: often a single line, sometimes just a few words, some taken straight from scripture or from old prayers. Second, they repeat, sometimes for several minutes. The repetition is the point.
Once nobody has to think about the next verse, attention can go somewhere else. Third, the languages.

The chants are sung in many languages, including Latin, some of them very old words in new music. Ubi caritas is an old Latin hymn text: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est," where charity and love are, God is there.
Others echo the Psalms, like Psalm 117: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people."
Fourth, the silence in the middle.

teach.h: UBI CARITAS ET AMOR, DEUS IBI EST.
teach.b: A Taizé prayer usually has a Bible reading and then a long silence, set among the chants. The brothers have said they hope a chant keeps going after the prayer ends, hummed under the breath while working or walking.
That's how a short line becomes a companion for the day.

how: At Taizé and in Taizé-style services elsewhere, people sing short chants many times over, hear a short Bible reading, and keep a long silence together, often by candlelight.

games.q: you have sung the same short line over and over at evening prayer in Taizé. it ends. what comes next?
o: a new hymn with several verses.
games.why: the line starts again. the repetition is the point: once nobody has to think about the next verse, attention can go somewhere else.

practice: Choose one line: if you pray, Ubi caritas, or any short line you already know from your own tradition; if not, a single line of any song that steadies you.
Hum or sing it softly, let it end, and start it again, same tune, same words. By the third or fourth time, notice whether you're still reading it in your head, or just singing it.
